summary: Specifies a protocol for encapsulating an arbitrary network layer protocol inside another arbitrary network layer protocol. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: It is like putting one envelope inside another so a message can travel across a network that does not understand it.

questions: how does generic routing encapsulation work
what is the gre header format
what ip protocol number does gre use
subtitle: A simple, general wrapper for carrying one network-layer protocol inside another.

tldr.problem: Many separate "X over Y" encapsulation schemes existed, and each new pairing needed its own specification.
tldr.mechanism: GRE puts a small header in front of the payload packet, with a Protocol Type naming what the payload is and an optional checksum. The result rides inside any delivery protocol, such as IPv4 (protocol 47).
tldr.outcome: It documents the subset of GRE that multiple vendors had deployed. It is updated by RFC 2890 and RFC 9601, and leaves several issues open, including Path MTU discovery and IPv6.

today: RFC 2784 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 2890 and RFC 9601. The text itself describes only version 0 GRE as deployed by multiple vendors at the time and lists IPv6 and Path MTU Discovery among the issues it leaves open.

sections.title: Why a General Encapsulation
sections.content:
Several proposals already existed for encapsulating one protocol over another, such as IPX over IP and AX.25 frames over IP, plus schemes for carrying IP over IP for policy purposes. GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) is similar to these but more general. It tries to reduce the encapsulation problem from its current O(n^2) size to a more manageable one.

The RFC admits the cost of generality: because many protocol-specific nuances are ignored, GRE may be less suitable where a specific "X over Y" encapsulation has already been described. It also purposely does not say when a packet should be encapsulated.

The packet being wrapped is the payload packet. It is wrapped in a GRE packet, which can then be carried by an outer delivery protocol. The RFC describes the intersection of GRE as currently deployed by multiple vendors.
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing a new special envelope for every pair of mail systems, GRE offers one all-purpose envelope that works for many of them.

sections.title: Structure of a GRE Packet
sections.content:
A GRE packet has three layers, outermost first: the delivery header, the GRE header and the payload packet. The specification is mostly about the GRE header, with some special attention to IPv4 payloads.

The header begins with a C (Checksum Present) bit, then the Reserved0 bits, a 3-bit Ver field and a 16-bit Protocol Type. If the C bit is set, a 16-bit Checksum and a 16-bit Reserved1 field follow.
sections.eli5: The parcel has an outer wrapper that gets it across the network, a GRE label saying what is inside, and then the original parcel itself.

sections.title: The GRE Header Fields
sections.content:
If the Checksum Present bit (bit 0) is one, the Checksum and Reserved1 fields are present, and a compliant implementation MUST accept and process the checksum.

Reserved0 covers bits 1 to 12. A receiver MUST discard a packet where any of bits 1 to 5 are non-zero, unless it implements RFC 1701. Bits 6 to 12 are reserved: they MUST be sent as zero and MUST be ignored on receipt. The Version field (bits 13 to 15) MUST contain zero.

Protocol Type holds the type of the payload, using the values defined as "ETHER TYPES". A receiver that sees a Protocol Type not listed there SHOULD discard the packet.

The Checksum is the IP (one's complement) checksum of all the 16-bit words in the GRE header and the payload packet, computed with the checksum field itself set to zero. Reserved1 MUST be sent as zero and exists only when the checksum does.
sections.eli5: The label has a box that says "what is inside" and an optional check number to catch damage. Boxes marked "reserved" must be left blank.

sections.title: IPv4 as Payload and Delivery Protocol
sections.content:
When IPv4 is the GRE payload, the Protocol Type MUST be 0x800. When a tunnel endpoint decapsulates such a packet, it MUST forward it using the destination address of the inner IPv4 header, and it MUST decrement the TTL of the payload packet.

Looping is possible if the payload's destination address is the encapsulator itself, that is, the other end of the tunnel. In that case the packet MUST be discarded.

When GRE is carried over IPv4, the delivery packet uses IPv4 protocol number 47. Requirements for delivering packets over IPv4 networks are in RFC 1122.
sections.eli5: When the parcel inside is an ordinary internet packet, the tunnel exit sends it onward like normal. If it is addressed back to the tunnel's own start, it is thrown away so it does not go round in circles.

sections.title: Compatibility with RFC 1701
sections.content:
In the earlier GRE of RFC 1701, the field now called Reserved0 held flag bits. This specification deprecates the Routing Present, Key Present, Sequence Number Present and Strict Source Route bits, along with the Recursion Control field. A header therefore never contains the Key, Sequence Number or Routing fields of RFC 1701.

An RFC 1701 receiver reading a packet from a sender following this specification sees those bits as zero and does not expect the extra fields. In the other direction, an RFC 1701 transmitter may set those bits and send the extra fields, which is why a receiver not implementing RFC 1701 MUST discard packets with any of bits 1 to 5 set.
sections.eli5: An older version of the label had extra boxes. The new label leaves them blank, so old readers still understand it, and new readers refuse labels that use the old boxes.

sections.title: Security and Known Issues
sections.content:
Security with GRE should be relatively similar to a normal IPv4 network, because routing with GRE follows the same routing IPv4 uses natively. Packet filtering is the difference: a firewall must either look inside the GRE packet or filtering must be done at the tunnel endpoints. Where this is a concern, it may be desirable to terminate the tunnel at the firewall.

An appendix lists known issues that the document does not address. Existing IPv4-delivered GRE does not implement Path MTU Discovery and does not set the Don't Fragment bit, so large packets can be fragmented within the tunnel and reassembled at its exit. IPv6 as delivery or payload protocol is not included. Interaction with ICMP, with the Differentiated Services Architecture, and multiple and looping encapsulations are also listed as open.
sections.eli5: Because the real parcel is hidden inside, a guard checking parcels at a gate has to open the outer wrapper first. Some problems, like very big parcels, were left for later.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This document specifies GRE version number 0. GRE version number 1 is used by PPTP (RFC 2637). Additional version numbers are assigned by IETF Consensus under RFC 2434.

GRE reuses ETHER Types for its Protocol Type field, and new ETHER Types are assigned by Xerox Systems Institute.
sections.eli5: Version numbers and type codes are handed out by a central list so two different groups do not use the same code for different things.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: Checksum Present; if one, Checksum and Reserved1 are present.

fields.name: Reserved0
fields.desc: Bits 1-5 non-zero means discard (unless RFC 1701); bits 6-12 sent as zero.

fields.name: Protocol Type
fields.desc: Protocol type of the payload packet, an ETHER TYPE.

fields.name: Checksum (optional)
fields.desc: One's complement checksum of the GRE header and payload.

fields.name: Reserved1 (optional)
fields.desc: Reserved; MUST be transmitted as zero.
